cards.title: Justify every campaign beyond one (justification-based account structure)
cards.summary: Build Google Ads accounts around one default consolidated campaign and require a commercial justification for each added campaign.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing the account structure for a store's Google Shopping/Search program and deciding whether to split into more campaigns.
steps: Treat one campaign as the theoretical default, acknowledge it is rarely realistic, and require heavy justification for every additional campaign layered on top.

Segment only for one of the four valid reasons: (1) brand vs non-brand search so brand placements don't share budget with cold acquisition, (2) geography when selling to multiple countries, (3) different margin or efficiency goals, (4) genuinely different product categories that learn toward different personas.

Split on margin specifically because Google bids on revenue, not profit: a 70% gross-margin collection and a 35% gross-margin collection cannot share one tROAS target, since the high-revenue, lower-margin collection will absorb the spend even when barely profitable at that target.
Use the office-chairs-vs-plants example as the test for category splits: if two products share a plausible use case but attract different buyer personas, segment so each learns in isolation.
When no justification applies, consolidate rather than segment to avoid reducing performance for the sake of complexity.
caveats: The source's '70% vs 35% margin' numbers are illustrative examples of the margin-segmentation principle, not a threshold formula.
The four justifications are the source's framework, not a universal rule.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Route 80-90% of ecommerce spend to Shopping, not Search
cards.summary: Ecommerce and retail accounts should put most spend into Shopping because pre-click information improves traffic quality.
cards.use_when: Deciding budget allocation between Shopping and Search campaigns for an ecommerce store.
steps: Aim for 80-90% of spend in Shopping for ecom/retail, reserving Search for additional volume once Shopping saturates.

Reason: Search ads show only a headline, an unread description and extensions — no image, price, variants or brand cues — so users click on faith and land on the wrong product, producing worse conversion rates.
Shopping listings show image, price, title, promos/reviews and competitor listings side by side, so the user pre-compares across ~6 listings and pre-selects the most relevant one before clicking.

Exception: ecommerce businesses with a B2B component often perform better on Search, because business buyers making bulk/supplier purchases distrust Shopping price listings and click Search ads instead.
caveats: The 80-90% figure is the source's rule of thumb, not a guaranteed optimum.
Shopping outperforms Search 'until you completely saturate the Shopping network' per the source.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Use single-topic ad groups (STAG) instead of SKAGs
cards.summary: Replace single-keyword ad groups with themed ad groups holding 10-20 related keywords and theme-tuned ads.
cards.use_when: Building or restructuring Search campaign ad groups for a store's keyword themes.
steps: Group 10-20 thematically related keywords per ad group (e.g. 'general plumbing', 'emergency plumbing', 'affordable plumbing' as separate themed groups).
Tune the ad copy in each group to that theme so it is contextually relevant to every keyword in the group.

Abandon SKAGs: responsive search ads have ~2,700 asset combinations and need ~250,000 impressions to properly test, which a single exact-match keyword can never deliver, keeping the ad in permanent learning.
Tie consolidation to scale: higher volume through the ad group/ad level is the only way for the campaign to exit learning.
Reject Google/Facebook advice by default, but treat consolidation of keywords as the minority of platform advice worth testing — the source reports it wins across all accounts they work on.
caveats: Responsive search ads are now the only ad type available in Search (per source at time of recording); verify current Google Ads interface.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Structure PMax asset groups by product type with matched listing groups
cards.summary: Build 3-20 PMax asset groups segmented by product type, each with its own customized listing group of at least 15 products.
cards.use_when: Setting up or fixing a Performance Max campaign for an ecommerce catalog.
steps: Default PMax creates one asset group — actively build multiple, remembering the asset group is the ad-unit equivalent (like a Meta ad) and the listing group is the feed-product bundle.

Customize the listing group inside each asset group so the products match the assets (a jeans asset group holds only jeans products); forgetting this lumps all products into every group and defeats the segmentation.
Segment by product type (furniture: chairs/tables/lighting/decor; hardware: hand tools/power tools/fasteners/accessories).
Ensure at least 15 products per asset group; never a single product (it may get starved of spend).
Enforce the rule as minimum 3 asset groups, maximum ~20 — past 20, most businesses lack the complexity to justify it, and simpler structures won repeatedly in the source's tests.
caveats: The 15-product floor and 3-20 range are source-stated heuristics, adjustable to catalog size.
The source ran tests up to ~200 hyper-segmented asset groups; simpler always won.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Diagnose why PMax segmentation is worth breaking consolidation
cards.summary: Use four concrete benefits to decide whether splitting PMax asset groups is justified for a store.
cards.use_when: Justifying or rejecting PMax asset-group segmentation for a specific product category set.
steps: Creative relevance (retargeting): segment so a user who viewed jeans is retargeted with jeans imagery/headlines across Display/YouTube, not random fashion products.
Cold creative relevance: PMax places cold on Display/YouTube; segmented feeds let it serve jeans to in-market-for-jeans users rather than the entire catalog to anyone interested in the brand.
Audience signals: set granular signals per asset group; per the source these are directional inputs for launching (not Meta-style targeting) and Google bypasses them once real conversion data exists.
Search themes: feed in actual historically converting search terms from your account rather than invented keywords; also signal-only, not targeting.
Performance visibility: segmentation lets you read which product types outperform (e.g. tops beating jeans seasonally) and reallocate.
caveats: Source ran PMax on 250+ accounts and consulted on ~400 ecom accounts; they report audience signals/search themes are near-irrelevant (1% at best) for mature accounts spending $30-100k+/month, mattering only at new launches. Treat as source opinion, not law.
Verify current Google Ads interface for brand/negative options, which change frequently.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Set brand exclusions (two ways) on PMax to stop pure retargeting
cards.summary: Always exclude branded traffic from PMax so the campaign cannot over-credit warm/repeat conversions.
cards.use_when: Configuring PMax campaigns and auditing whether brand traffic is inflating reported ROAS.
steps: Apply a brand list exclusion via campaign settings → brand exclusions → add new brand; Google indexes and finds branded terms, then apply the list.
Also add brand terms as negative keywords now that PMax supports them, and apply BOTH as fail-safes — brand list catches missed variations, negatives protect if the list fails.
Recognize that a PMax without brand exclusions is effectively a retargeting campaign.

Rank PMax levers by importance per the source: (1) GMC feed titles/descriptions/imagery (when PMax prioritizes Shopping), (2) brand exclusions, (3) asset & listing group structure plus copy, (4) bidding strategy, (5) audience signals and search themes.
caveats: Negative-keyword support in PMax is a relatively recent rollout; verify current availability in your account.
An unaudited account may still be the right call if the campaign is genuinely driving cold acquisition.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Run feed-only PMax to force Shopping placement and fix runaway spend
cards.summary: Delete asset groups to create a feed-only PMax that can only serve Shopping + Display retargeting, controlling misrouted spend.
cards.use_when: When PMax is over-spending on Gmail/YouTube or you want to force spend into Shopping placement.
steps: Delete the asset groups — only the listing group (GMC feed) remains, so PMax can only place on Shopping and Display remarketing (the old Smart Shopping behavior).
Turn OFF URL expansion in settings, or PMax scrapes/auto-builds URLs and asset groups itself.
Turn OFF automatically created assets, or PMax fabricates assets and defeats the feed-only constraint.

Use case from source: a client spending a couple hundred thousand/month on PMax saw clicks spike and ROAS drop ~20% as spend shifted to YouTube (2% → 10%) and Gmail cold (10%); going feed-only blocked those placements and fixed the issue.
caveats: Source notes Gmail 'clicks' count email opens, not outbound website clicks — inflated click volume is a signal to check placements.
Feed-only is a context-dependent nuance; the source does not prescribe it universally.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Move to tROAS for stability, then avoid the over-tightening trap
cards.summary: Start on max conversion value for data, roll into target ROAS for day-to-day reliability, and watch for the tROAS trap of throttling cold reach.
cards.use_when: Choosing and tuning a bidding strategy for a store's PMax/Shopping campaigns.
steps: Launch on max conversion value to accumulate data, then transition to target ROAS; the source says the average performance over the period is similar, but tROAS flattens week-to-week volatility.
Set the initial tROAS slightly below trailing ROAS (e.g. trailing ~420-430% → set ~400%).
If budget is capped, raising tROAS squeezes efficiency but shrinks the targetable audience toward warmer users — efficiency looks better while genuine new-customer acquisition falls.
Diagnose with a mental cold/warm pool: higher tROAS = smaller circle = warmer; scaling spend = larger circle = colder and less efficient.
Do not over-optimize tROAS to chase a headline number; the source says the lower, less 'impressive' tROAS was likely the better position.
caveats: Smart bidding requires sufficient conversion data; brand-new accounts with no data are forced onto manual bidding (verify current eligibility).
The stability-vs-performance trade is the source's account of observed platform behavior, not a guarantee.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Build a feeder strategy: cold funnel campaign feeding a high-tROAS retargeter
cards.summary: Run a very low-tROAS cold campaign to cheaply reach under-bid auctions, then convert that traffic with a high-tROAS campaign.
cards.use_when: When you need genuine cold acquisition in Google that PMax over-attributes on its own.
steps: Set up a cold campaign (standard Shopping, per source) at a very low tROAS (source example: 50%/0.5x) to reach the whole pool of users searching relevant terms — including the low-intent half almost no one bids on.
Set up a second campaign at high tROAS (source example: 600%) to retarget the warm pool that the first campaign fed.
Confirm the arbitrage premise: most high-tROAS bidders compete only for the high-intent half, so the low-intent auctions are cheap to win.

Expect the first campaign's in-platform attribution to look weak and the second to look strong; per source, PMax 'substantially overattributes' (~50%+ of conversions are repeat/warm) while standard Shopping underattributes because PMax takes the final click.
caveats: The 50%/600% figures are source examples, not recommended universal settings.
The source states ~50%+ PMax conversions being warm/repeat is their finding across agencies, presented as opinion, not a published benchmark.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Standard Shopping structures: top-sellers split, feeder, and labelizer
cards.summary: Three in-market Shopping structures plus when each is (and isn't) worth the complexity.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to organize standard Shopping campaigns for a store's catalog.
steps: Top-sellers split: put top sellers in one campaign and everything else in another, forcing ~80% of spend into the top 20% of products while keeping testing budget on the rest to roll up new winners. Only for non-fashion catalogs with a large SKU count; not for fashion and not for 5-10 product stores.
Feeder strategy: standard Shopping as the cold acquisition layer feeding a high-tROAS campaign (see feeder card).

Labelizer: split products into over-index / index / near-index / under-index / no-index tiers with custom labels, either manually (small catalogs) or via an automated labelizer script that re-tiers on 30-day rolling performance and assigns tier-appropriate bids/budgets.
Default to consolidation; apply the four justification variables (brand/non-brand, geography, margin/efficiency, category) before segmenting.
caveats: The source explicitly does not recommend labelizer for most businesses — it adds segmentation with limited upside unless you have thousands of SKUs.
Segment based on the four justification variables, not on arbitrary splits.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Run Search campaigns only for the right cases; use STAGs and front-load negatives
cards.summary: Search is secondary for most ecom, but essential with B2B — structure with topic ad groups and aggressive early negative-keyword policing.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest in Search and how to police it for a store.
steps: For 90% of ecom brands, put ~90% of focus into Shopping; add Search for additional volume after Shopping saturates.
Exception: ecom with a B2B component often performs better on Search (bulk/supplier buyers distrust Shopping price listings).
Use single-topic ad groups (themed keywords, theme-tuned ads) rather than SKAGs.

Front-load negative keywords in the first 30 days — highest-leverage window because the campaign goes broad; review weekly (or daily at high budget) then drop to weekly-ish, avoiding over-tweaking which resets learnings.
Maintain a universal account-level negative list inherited by every new campaign (job/careers/intern/hiring/salary terms, etc.); source suggests a pre-made list or building one with an LLM.
Always exclude brand on Search campaigns; typically use smart bidding (tROAS, max conversions).
caveats: Review cadence ('weekly', 'daily at high budget') is source guidance, not a fixed rule.
Confirm negative-keyword tooling and bidding eligibility in the current Google Ads interface.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Treat landing-page testing as the biggest Search lever
cards.summary: A/B test landing pages within ad groups over 30-60 days to raise conversion rate and unlock higher bids.
cards.use_when: Running acquisition on Google and looking to increase conversion rate and winning auctions.
steps: In an ad group/campaign, run two ads pointing to two different landing pages.
Monitor conversion rate over 30-60 days; keep the higher-converting landing page.
Rotate in a third landing-page test against the winner, turn off the loser, and repeat — compounding the account's average conversion rate.

Tie this to auction economics: Google is ultimately an auction of who can pay the most; 2x conversion rate lets you spend ~2x per click at the same return, and higher AOV squeezes more revenue from the same clicks.
Treat CPC as a vanity metric: across large datasets CPC and ROI show little relationship in the middle range (extremes aside), so don't optimize for lowest CPC.
Add AOV optimization alongside CVR for compounding leverage.
caveats: The 30-60 day test window and '2x CVR → 2x click budget' are the source's reasoning, not a measured guarantee.
The CPC-ROI relationship conclusion is the source's observation from its own account analyses.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx

cards.title: Fix seven common Google Ads account hygiene mistakes
cards.summary: Audit and correct frequent account-level setup errors that waste budget or distort attribution.
cards.use_when: Auditing an ecommerce Google Ads account for structural errors before scaling.
steps: Do not use GA4 events as the primary conversion — the source reports a ~10-15% (sometimes higher) attribution gap versus direct snippet code; use the direct snippet for the primary conversion.
Never run just one asset group on PMax — enforce segmentation at the asset-group level.
Do not run broad match with maximize clicks — broad match requires a smart bidding strategy to work.
Disable Display in Search campaigns, especially for cold traffic.
Add branded negatives on cold campaigns plus general negatives on Search campaigns.
Turn off Google's auto-apply recommendations — they almost always act against your interest.

Apply a proper naming convention so anyone can read context: agency tag → region → campaign type (PMax/Shopping/Search) → audience (cold/brand/theta) → goal (usually dropped, since it's conversions 99% of the time).
caveats: The 10-15% GA4 attribution gap is the source's reported figure; verify against your own setup.
Some items (auto-apply behavior, broad match requirements) can change with platform updates — recheck the current interface.
cards.source_name: How to Scale an eCommerce Brand Profitably in 2026_ The Full System.docx
